module.title: Habitual Past & Adaptations: Used To vs Would vs Be/Get Used To
module.objective: Menguasai perbedaan kebiasaan masa lalu (used to / would) dengan proses adaptasi kebiasaan baru (be/get used to + V-ing).

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Habitual Past & Life Changes
subModules.theme: Personal Habits, Childhood Memories, and Adapting to New Environments
subModules.grammarFocus: Used To vs Would vs Be/Get Used To

content.summary: Welcome to Unit B1.2-M09. In this reading mission, you will explore how people talk about past habits that no longer happen and how they describe the process of adapting to brand new routines. Through engaging texts and targeted rules, you will learn the exact differences between 'used to', 'would', and 'be/get used to'.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Distinguishing between past states, repeated past actions, and the current state or process of familiarity.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Key terms related to personal adjustments, daily routines, commuting, and lifestyle transitions.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning texts for specific grammatical structures and skimming paragraphs to grasp the overall story of personal adaptation.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short B1 texts about personal changes and childhood memories.
Locate specific details regarding past routines versus current adjustments.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns with used to, would, be used to, and get used to.

contextWarmup.prompt: When you start a new school or a new job, what is usually the hardest part to get comfortable with?
options: Learning the new daily commute and waking up earlier
Remembering the names of the buildings
Eating lunch at a different time
contextWarmup.explanation: Adapting to a new daily schedule and commute requires significant adjustment, making it one of the most common challenges when starting a new routine.

rules: USED TO + infinitive: Expresses past habits or states that are no longer true today. Formula: Subject + used to + verb (infinitive). Example: 'I used to live in Jakarta' (now I do not).

WOULD + infinitive: Expresses repeated actions in the past, but cannot be used for past states or situations. Formula: Subject + would + verb (infinitive). Example: 'Every weekend, we would go to the beach.'
BE USED TO + gerund/noun: Expresses being familiar with something because of time or experience. Formula: Subject + be + used to + V-ing/noun. Example: 'I am used to waking up early.'
GET USED TO + gerund/noun: Expresses the active process of becoming familiar with something new. Formula: Subject + get + used to + V-ing/noun. Example: 'I am getting used to working from home.'

commonTrap.explanation: Students often confuse 'used to do' (past habit) with 'be used to doing' (familiarity) or misuse 'would' for past states.
commonTrap.wrong: I would live in a small town when I was a child.
commonTrap.correct: I used to live in a small town when I was a child. ('Live' is a state, so 'would' is incorrect).

grammarFormulas.description: Assemble sentence blocks to practice affirmative, negative, and question forms:

complements.text: getting used to the new commute

items.exampleSentence: It took me several weeks to adapt to the new work environment.
Moving to a new country requires a big adjustment in your daily routine.
I used to have a very strict morning routine when I was younger.
I am still getting used to the long commute to my new office.
Initially, I found it difficult to work remotely, but now I am used to it.

I can still recall the days when we would play outside every afternoon.

content.passageTitle: Embracing Change: From Past Habits to New Beginnings
paragraphs: Looking back at my childhood, I can easily recall how simple life used to be. Every summer, my family and I would travel to a small coastal village where we spent hours swimming in the ocean. I used to think those sunny days would last forever. Back then, my daily routine was completely carefree, and I never worried about schedules or responsibilities.

However, moving to the city for university brought a massive transition. Initially, the lifestyle adjustment was overwhelming. The city atmosphere felt loud and busy compared to my quiet hometown. I struggled with the long commute to campus every morning, and waking up at six o'clock was exhausting. Fortunately, humans are designed to adapt. Over the last few months, I have gradually gotten used to the fast pace of city life, and now I even enjoy the energetic vibe of my new routine.

questions.question: What does the author remember about childhood summers in the passage?
options: Traveling to a small coastal village and swimming for hours
Working part-time in a busy city office
Studying hard for university entrance exams
questions.answer: Traveling to a small coastal village and swimming for hours
questions.explanation: The passage states that every summer the family would travel to a small coastal village where they spent hours swimming in the ocean.

questions.question: Which grammar structure does the author use to describe past summer trips?
options: Would + infinitive
Be used to + V-ing
Get used to + noun
questions.explanation: The text uses 'would travel' and 'would spend' to describe repeated actions in the past.

questions.question: How did the author describe the initial lifestyle adjustment after moving to the city?
options: Overwhelming
Relaxing
Boring
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explicitly states that initially, the lifestyle adjustment was overwhelming.

questions.question: What part of city life did the author struggle with every morning?
options: The long commute to campus
Finding a place to eat lunch
Meeting new professors
questions.explanation: The text mentions struggling with the long commute to campus every morning.

questions.question: Which phrase describes the author's current state regarding city life?
options: Have gradually gotten used to the fast pace
Used to live in a coastal village
Would hate waking up early
questions.answer: Have gradually gotten used to the fast pace
questions.explanation: The text states the author has gradually gotten used to the fast pace of city life.

questions.question: What does 'recall' mean in the context of the passage?
options: To remember something from the past
To buy something new
To forget completely
questions.answer: To remember something from the past
questions.explanation: To recall means to bring a fact, event, or situation back into one's mind, similar to remembering.

questions.question: Why is 'would' not suitable for describing past states like 'living in a small town'?
options: Because would is only used for repeated physical actions, not states or permanent situations
Because would is only used in present tense sentences
Because would can only be used with questions
questions.answer: Because would is only used for repeated physical actions, not states or permanent situations
questions.explanation: Grammar rules dictate that 'would' describes repeated past actions, whereas 'used to' can describe both past actions and past states.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between 'be used to' and 'get used to'?
options: 'Be used to' describes a current state of familiarity, while 'get used to' describes the process of adapting
'Be used to' is for the future, while 'get used to' is for the past
There is no difference between the two expressions
questions.answer: 'Be used to' describes a current state of familiarity, while 'get used to' describes the process of adapting
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' means you are already comfortable, whereas 'get used to' highlights the transition or process of becoming comfortable.

questions.question: Which word from the vocabulary bank means 'a sudden or major change from one state to another'?
options: Transition
Atmosphere
Routine
questions.explanation: Transition refers to the process or a period of changing from one state or condition to another.

questions.question: Based on the reading passage, how does the author feel about their new routine now?
options: They enjoy the energetic vibe of their new life
They want to move back to the coastal village immediately
They still find waking up at six o'clock impossible
questions.answer: They enjoy the energetic vibe of their new life
questions.explanation: The final sentence notes that the author now even enjoys the energetic vibe of their new routine.

content.summary: Listen for specific grammar markers that distinguish past habits from ongoing adaptation. Focus on how speakers contrast their past routines using used to and would with their current state of adjusting using be or get used to followed by a gerund.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about personal changes and city life.
Identify details such as past routines versus current adjustments.
Notice how words link together in connected speech during natural rapid dialogue.

keyPhrases.note: Used to describe an ongoing adaptation process to a new situation.
Used for repeated past actions or typical behavior in the past.
Used for past states or habits that are no longer true.

connectedSpeech.note: The vowel in to reduces to a schwa, and the final d blends into the following vowel.
The phrase flows smoothly without pausing between words.
Consonant blending connects the final d of would with the g of get.
Linking consonants to vowels creates a continuous rhythm.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Past Habits and Personal Adaptations

content.summary: Clear guidelines for writing about past habits using used to and would, and explaining adaptation using be or get used to.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Stating Past Habits and States
blueprintItems.example: I used to play the piano when I was a child.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Describing Repeated Past Actions
blueprintItems.example: Every summer, we would visit our grandparents in the countryside.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Expressing Familiarity or Adaptation
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + be/get + used to + verb-ing or noun
blueprintItems.example: She is getting used to waking up early for her new job.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use the base verb after used to in negative sentences and questions.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I didn't used to like coffee.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I didn't use to like coffee.
mechanicsRules.why: In negative sentences with did not, the verb use loses the letter d.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not use would with state verbs for past habits.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I would live in a small village.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I used to live in a small village.
mechanicsRules.why: State verbs like live, be, or have describe states, not actions, so only used to is correct.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always follow used to in adaptation phrases with a gerund or noun.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I am used to wake up early.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I am used to waking up early.
mechanicsRules.why: The word to in be used to and get used to is a preposition, so it requires a noun or a verb ending in ing.

sampleSentences.en: My grandfather used to smoke, but he stopped ten years ago.
sampleSentences.id: Kakek saya dulu merokok, tetapi beliau berhenti sepuluh tahun lalu.
sampleSentences.focus: Past habit that no longer exists

sampleSentences.en: On snowy winter mornings, we would drink hot chocolate by the window.
sampleSentences.id: Pada pagi hari musim dingin yang bersalju, kami biasanya minum cokelat panas di dekat jendela.

sampleSentences.en: It was difficult at first, but now I am used to driving on the left side.
sampleSentences.id: Awalnya sulit, tetapi sekarang saya sudah terbiasa menyetir di sisi kiri.

sampleSentences.en: He is getting used to the noisy traffic in the city center.
sampleSentences.id: Dia sedang membiasakan diri dengan lalu lintas yang bising di pusat kota.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Use 'used to' instead of 'would' for past states.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Follow 'be used to' with a gerund ending in ing.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Childhood Memories
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three sentences about things you used to do or would do when you were a child. Use both 'used to' and 'would' where appropriate.
guidedLabChallenges.example: I used to have a red bicycle. Every afternoon, I would ride it around the neighborhood. My friends would join me after school.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Adapting to Changes

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the correct form of used to:
practicumQuestions.promptText: I lived in Paris when I was a child, but I live in London now.
targetAnswers: I used to live in Paris when I was a child.
I used to live in Paris.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'used to' followed by the base verb 'live' to describe a past state that is no longer true.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the affirmative sentence into a negative sentence using used to:
practicumQuestions.promptText: She ate vegetables when she was younger.
targetAnswers: She didn't use to eat vegetables when she was younger.
She didn't use to eat vegetables.
practicumQuestions.explanation: In negative sentences, use 'didn't use to' with the base verb 'eat'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the error in the following sentence about a past habit:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Did you used to have long hair?
practicumQuestions.hint: Check the spelling of the auxiliary question form.
targetAnswers: Did you use to have long hair?
practicumQuestions.explanation: In questions with 'did', the correct form is 'did you use to', not 'did you used to'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Choose between would and used to for this state verb sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Complete: I _____ (be) very shy when I was a teenager.
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember that state verbs cannot use would.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The verb 'be' is a state verb. State verbs take 'used to', never 'would'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the repeated past action using would:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Every Sunday, we visited our grandparents and baked cookies together.
targetAnswers: Every Sunday, we would visit our grandparents and baked cookies together.
Every Sunday, we would visit our grandparents and would bake cookies together.
practicumQuestions.explanation: We can use 'would' to describe repeated actions in the past when the time frame is clear.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using be used to with a gerund:
practicumQuestions.promptText: I am familiar with working night shifts now.
targetAnswers: I am used to working night shifts.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Familiarity with a routine is expressed using 'be used to' followed by the gerund 'working'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using get used to to show the process of adaptation:
practicumQuestions.promptText: It is becoming normal for me to wake up early.
targetAnswers: I am getting used to waking up early.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The process of adaptation over time is expressed using 'get used to' + gerund.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the grammar error in this adaptation sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: She is used to live in a cold climate.
practicumQuestions.hint: The preposition 'to' must be followed by a gerund.
targetAnswers: She is used to living in a cold climate.
practicumQuestions.explanation: After 'be used to', the verb must be in the gerund form ending in ing ('living').

practicumQuestions.instruction: Answer the question in a complete sentence using used to: What did you do after school when you were ten?
practicumQuestions.promptText: I / play / video games with my brother.
targetAnswers: I used to play video games with my brother.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Form a complete sentence using 'I used to play' to describe a past habit.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Answer the question in a complete sentence using get used to: Are you comfortable with the new software yet?
practicumQuestions.promptText: Yes, / I / get / used to / it / now.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use present continuous: 'am getting used to it'.
targetAnswers: Yes, I am getting used to it now.
Yes, I am getting used to it.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'am getting used to' to show that you are in the process of adapting to the new software.

content.summary: Mastering the spoken forms of past habits and ongoing adjustments requires clear linking, proper sentence stress, and precise articulation of weak forms like 'to' and 'would'.
content.audioGuidance: Pay close attention to how 'used to' is pronounced as /juːstə/ in connected speech. The final 'd' of 'used' blends smoothly into the 'to', dropping the hard stop.

pillars.name: Weak Form Articulation
pillars.explanation: Native speakers rarely pronounce 'used to' with a full vowel sound on 'to'. Keep it weak and quick to maintain a natural conversational rhythm.

pillars.name: Sentence Stress for Contrast
pillars.target: Stressing new habits versus past states
pillars.explanation: When contrasting past habits with current adjustments, place stress on auxiliary verbs like 'am', 'is', or 'get' in 'getting used to'.

pillars.name: Intonation in Explanations
pillars.target: Using falling intonation for completed past routines
pillars.explanation: End statements about past states with a falling pitch to signal that the habit has finished and is no longer part of your present life.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The primary stress remains on the first syllable in both base forms.
Stress shifts slightly when adding suffixes, maintaining prominence on the second syllable root.
Both nouns have stress on the final syllable.
Adverb stress placement varies depending on the root word structure.

drills.focus: Expression 'getting used to' followed by a noun phrase
drills.hint: Emphasize 'getting' and 'used' to highlight the ongoing adaptation process.

drills.phonetic: /ʃiː faʊnd ɪt hɑːd æt fɜːst, bʌt naʊ ʃiː ɪz ˈjuːst tʊ ˈwɜːkɪŋ əˈləʊn/
drills.focus: Contrasting past difficulty with present comfort using 'is used to'

roleplay.context: You meet your former colleague at a cafe and discuss how your daily routines have changed.

turns.speaker: Colleague
turns.text: It is so good to see you! Do you still work the night shift like you did last year?
turns.translation: Senang sekali bisa bertemu denganmu! Apakah kamu masih bekerja shift malam seperti tahun lalu?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: No, I changed jobs. I used to work nights, but now I am getting used to waking up early.
turns.translation: Tidak, saya pindah pekerjaan. Dulu saya biasa bekerja malam, tapi sekarang saya sedang membiasakan diri bangun pagi.

turns.speaker: Colleague
turns.text: That sounds like a big change. Was it difficult to adapt?
turns.translation: Itu terdengar seperti perubahan besar. Apakah sulit untuk beradaptasi?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Initially, it was exhausting. However, I gradually adapted to the morning routine.
turns.translation: Pada awalnya, itu sangat melelahkan. Namun, saya perlahan-lahan beradaptasi dengan rutinitas pagi.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 20 seconds about a childhood habit using 'used to' or 'would'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Describe a game or activity you used to do with your friends when you were younger.
storyPoints: What game or activity you played regularly in the past
Where you used to play and who joined you
How you feel now when you recall those memories
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: When I was young, we would play football in the street every single afternoon.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wɛn aɪ wɒz jʌŋ, wiː wʊd pleɪ ˈfʊtbɔːl ɪn ðə striːt ˈɛvri ˈsɪŋɡl ˈɑːftənuːn/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'would' or 'used to' to describe repeated past actions with clear pronunciation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 20 seconds about a major lifestyle adjustment you made recently.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell me about a new routine you had to adopt recently and how you adjusted to it.
storyPoints: What the new routine or environment is
Why it felt difficult or strange at first
How you are currently getting used to it
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I recently started a new job, and I am still getting used to the early morning commute.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ ˈriːsntli ˈstɑːtɪd ə njuː dʒɒb, ænd aɪ æm stɪl ˈɡɛtɪŋ ˈjuːst tʊ ðə ˈɜːli ˈmɔːnɪŋ kəˈmjuːt/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate the correct use of 'be getting used to' followed by a noun phrase.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond naturally to your friend asking about your childhood reading habits.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hey! Did you read a lot of books when you were a teenager?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A childhood friend asks about your past reading habits.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yes, I used to read adventure novels every night before going to sleep.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /jɛs, aɪ ˈjuːst tʊ riːd ədˈvɛntʃə ˈnɒvəlz ˈɛvri naɪt bɪˈfɔːr ˈɡəʊɪŋ tuː sliːp/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Answer the question directly using 'used to' with smooth linking.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond to a coworker asking about your adjustment to a new office software.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Are you comfortable using the new project management tool yet?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A coworker checks on your progress adapting to a new workplace tool.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Initially it was confusing, but I am finally getting used to the new interface.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪˈnɪʃəli ɪt wɒz kənˈfjuːzɪŋ, bʌt aɪ æm ˈfaɪnəli ˈɡɛtɪŋ ˈjuːst tʊ ðə njuː ˈɪntəfeɪs/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'getting used to' to express an ongoing adaptation process.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Reply to a neighbor asking about your move to a quieter neighborhood.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Do you miss the noise of the city center after moving out here?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A friendly neighbor asks if you have adapted to the quiet countryside.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: It was quiet at first, but I am now used to the peaceful atmosphere here.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪt wɒz ˈkwaɪət æt fɜːst, bʌt aɪ æm naʊ ˈjuːst tʊ ðə ˈpiːsfʊl ˈætməsfɪər hɪə/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate the use of 'be used to' to describe a settled state of comfort.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond to a teacher asking about your transition to higher-level English classes.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: How are you finding the pace of the advanced speaking lessons?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: An English instructor checks if you are comfortable with the lesson pace.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: It took time, but I gradually got used to speaking English without translating in my head.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪt tʊk taɪm, bʌt aɪ ˈɡrædʒuəli ɡɒt ˈjuːst tʊ ˈspiːkɪŋ ˈɪŋɡlɪʃ wɪˈaʊt trænzˈleɪtɪŋ ɪn maɪ hɛd/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'got used to' with a gerund to describe past adjustment over time.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Pronounce a sentence using the target vocabulary word 'adjustment' correctly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence clearly: Moving to another country requires a major adjustment.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Moving to another country requires a major adjustment in your daily routine.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈmuːvɪŋ tuː əˈnʌðə ˈkʌntri rɪˈkwaɪəz ə ˈmeɪdʒə ˈəʊvəhɔːl ɪn jʊə ˈdeɪli ruːˈtiːn/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Ensure the target vocabulary item 'adjustment' is articulated clearly with correct word stress.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Pronounce a sentence contrasting a past state with a present habit using 'used to' vs 'be used to'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence: I used to wake up late, but now I am used to waking up early.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I used to wake up late, but now I am used to waking up early.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ ˈjuːst tʊ weɪk ʌp leɪt, bʌt naʊ aɪ æm ˈjuːst tʊ ˈweɪkɪŋ ʌp ˈɜːli/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Accurately contrast 'used to + infinitive' with 'be used to + gerund'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Pronounce the target words focusing on correct syllable stress placement.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say these two words with correct stress: aDAPT and aDAPtation.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: It takes time to adapt to a new adaptation.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪt teɪks taɪm tuː əˈdæpt tuː ə njuː ædæpˈteɪʃən/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Place primary stress on the correct syllable for both the base verb and the noun form.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read the sentence aloud using falling intonation at the end of completed past habits.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read this sentence with a clear falling tone on the final phrase: We would gather by the fireplace every winter.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: We would gather by the fireplace every winter.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wiː wʊd ˈɡæðə baɪ ðə ˈfaɪəpleɪs ˈɛvri ˈwɪntə/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a falling pitch contour at the end of the sentence to show a completed, nostalgic past routine.
